content: Collinsonia canadensis, commonly known as Canada Horsebalm, Richweed, Hardhack, Heal-All, Horseweed, Ox-Balm, or Stone Root, is a perennial medicinal herb belonging to the mint family. This plant was first identified by Peter Collinson (1693–1768), an English merchant botanist who was passionate about introducing and cultivating new American plants in England. Despite its discovery, Collinsonia was not initially utilized in European or American medicine. According to a pamphlet by the Lloyd Brothers, it did not attract the attention of prominent medical observers of the time, such as the Bartons, Dunglison, Zollicoffer, and Griffith, likely because it lacked any prominent toxic or violent properties that would make it stand out. The plant has a distinctive odor, which herbalist David Winston described as resembling the scent of Lemon Pledge. It was only after observing its use in Native American medicine that Collinsonia canadensis was incorporated into the materia medica. By the 1850s, it was included in King’s American Dispensatory and Lee’s New York Plants. Lee noted that the bruised leaves had been used for many years as poultices for bruises and that the Thomsonian medical practitioners had referenced it in their writings. One reason for its delayed adoption in medicine was the difficulty in extracting its active components, which required prolonged processing. The root of Collinsonia canadensis is dark brown to nearly black, knotty, and very heavy, covered with tough, black, wire-like fibers. When fresh, the crushed root has a faint, peculiar odor that disappears upon drying. Internally, the dried root is white, odorless, and imparts little taste, even when chewed for an extended period. The active principles of the plant are challenging to extract, regardless of whether the root is finely ground or powdered. The process demands significant time for the constituents to dissolve, irrespective of the solvent used. Both the fresh and dried roots impart a deep red-brown color to any solvent that successfully extracts its full properties. This coloration arises from the fact that the plant’s medicinal virtues are concentrated in the rootlets, the brown epidermis, and the slightly colored underlying portions, all of which must be included to produce a representative preparation. According to Cook’s 1869 Physiomedical Dispensatory, Collinsonia canadensis belongs to the natural order Labiatae. The genus Collinsonia consists of strongly scented herbs with large, ovate, petiolate leaves and yellow flowers arranged in terminal, leafless, panicled racemes. The calyx is ten-striate, with a truncate and three-toothed upper lip and a two-cleft lower lip. The corolla is exserted and ringent, with two long-exserted stamens. Collinsonia canadensis is an indigenous plant that thrives in rich, moist woods and fields. Its stem is four-sided, three to four feet tall, and often smooth, though sometimes slightly pubescent. The leaves are few, thin, three to four inches long, and two to three inches broad, with an acuminate shape, coarsely serrated edges, and a base that is abrupt or subcordate. The flowers, which bloom from July to September, are large, loose, and arranged in compound racemes. The corolla is yellow with a green tinge, about half an inch or more in length, with an elongated and fringed lower lip that emits a lemon-like odor. The root of Collinsonia canadensis is medicinal and perennial, characterized by its knotty, rough, and very hard texture. It is dusky brown, with numerous slender fibers, and emits a somewhat unpleasant balsamic odor when fresh. Due to the confusion caused by similar common names, it is important to distinguish this particular Hardhack from the shrub Spirea tomentosa, as well as from Ptelia trifoliata and Scrophularia marylandica, which are also frequently referred to as Heal-All. Petersen’s Materia Medica describes the plant’s medicinal uses, noting its specific influence on the nervous system and mucous membranes. It alleviates congestion and improves capillary circulation, particularly in relaxed conditions of the mucous membranes in the throat and lower bowels. It is considered a valuable remedy for sore throat, laryngitis, and pharyngitis, especially when associated with relaxed and weakened capillary circulation. It can be effectively combined with other indicated remedies for atonic dyspepsia, catarrhal gastritis with poor circulation, and irritable heart conditions caused by weakness. In cases of hemorrhoids, when appropriately indicated, it is regarded as one of the best remedies. For such conditions, it is recommended to use small doses. Scudder also recommends it for nurse’s sore mouth, where it is effective in cases involving relaxed conditions and impaired capillary circulation in the affected areas. The typical dosage is 4 to 6 drops, except in cases of hemorrhoids, where smaller doses of ½ to 1 drop are more effective than larger doses.
